summary: Ocean Software was founded in Manchester in 1983 by David Ward and Jon Woods. It began as Spectrum Games, adopted the Ocean name, and became strongly associated with licensed film, television and arcade properties across the British home-computer market.
facts: Founded in 1983 by David Ward and Jon Woods.
The business initially used the name Spectrum Games before adopting Ocean.
Ocean acquired the Imagine label in late 1984 and used it for many arcade conversions.
note: The source-backed company facts are separate from the archive strengths, which summarise the Ocean games represented by CCG.

sources.label: Centre for Computing History — Ocean Software company profile

summary: The business that became Mastertronic was started in London late in 1983 and began trading on 1 April 1984. Its defining strategy was budget software at £1.99, backed by a distribution-led approach designed to place inexpensive games directly onto a wide range of retail shelves.
facts: The business was started late in 1983 and began trading on 1 April 1984.
Its standard UK launch price was £1.99 at a time when many games cost considerably more.
Its commercial strategy concentrated on distributors and retailers as well as consumer demand.
note: The historical source was written by former Mastertronic financial controller Anthony Guter and is preserved by the Mastertronic Collectors Archive.

sources.label: Mastertronic Collectors Archive — A History of Mastertronic
Mastertronic Collectors Archive — site provenance

summary: Firebird was created in 1984 by Telecomsoft, British Telecom's software division. The label published games for the Commodore 64 and other home computers, using both budget and premium ranges while Telecomsoft explored software publishing alongside early ideas for network-delivered content.
facts: Firebird was created by Telecomsoft in 1984.
The label published for the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and other systems.
Firebird used both premium and budget ranges rather than serving only one price band.
note: Only the institutional archive's documented points are presented as company facts; Firebird, Rainbird and Silverbird remain separate CCG routes.

sources.label: Play It Again digital heritage archive — Firebird Software

summary: US Gold brought a substantial number of American and arcade properties to European home-computer owners. Its catalogue spans sports, action games, conversions and licensed releases across both C64 and Amiga.
note: Re-release labels are linked only where they exist as separate publisher routes in the CCG archive.
facts: The Play It Again archive records that Geoff and Anne Brown founded U.S. Gold in 1984 to publish American games in the United Kingdom and arrange conversions for British home computers.
The CCG publisher index currently records 46 U.S. Gold games across Commodore 64 and Amiga, covering 1982 to 1992.

sources.label: Play It Again — U.S. Gold company history
Cheeky Commodore Gamer — complete publisher index

summary: Codemasters was founded in the 1980s by brothers David and Richard Darling. Its early output included sports games such as BMX Simulator for the Commodore 64, and the company first built its business around affordable releases for 8-bit home computers.
facts: Founded in the 1980s by David and Richard Darling.
BMX Simulator for the Commodore 64 was among its early sports titles.
Its early catalogue concentrated on budget-priced 8-bit games before later expansion.
note: The company facts use Codemasters' official EA studio history, with the independent Codemasters Archive supplying additional context on its early budget focus.

sources.label: Codemasters official EA studio history
The Codemasters Archive — company history

summary: System 3 became closely associated with polished action-adventure releases and strong presentation on the Commodore 64. Several of its games remain among the machine's most discussed later-1980s releases.
note: Publishing and development credits can differ between territories and versions; this page follows the archive's recorded publisher fields.
facts: System 3's official history says Mark Cale formed the British developer and publisher in 1982.
The CCG publisher index currently records nine System 3 games across Commodore 64 and Amiga, spanning 1987 to 1990.

sources.label: System 3 — official company story
Cheeky Commodore Gamer — complete publisher index

summary: Activision was founded in 1979 and developed, published and distributed interactive entertainment. Its CCG Commodore archive reflects only part of a much wider catalogue and includes early home-computer releases alongside later licensed and distributed titles.
facts: Activision was founded in 1979.
The company described its business as developing, publishing and distributing interactive entertainment.
Its historical operations included the United Kingdom alongside North America and other international markets.
note: Territorial publisher credits can differ, so CCG continues to display the publisher stored for each archived version rather than rewriting game records.

sources.label: Activision investor archive — company profile in 2002 announcement

summary: Electronic Arts was founded in 1982. Its first five games shipped on 20 May 1983, with packaging that placed creator names prominently on the front; that first group included Archon and M.U.L.E., both later released for the Commodore 64.
facts: Electronic Arts was founded in 1982.
Its first five games shipped on 20 May 1983.
Early packaging presented game creators prominently and included titles later released on the Commodore 64.
note: The factual history is drawn from EA's own company and anniversary pages; archive strengths describe the EA games currently represented by CCG.

sources.label: Electronic Arts — About EA
Electronic Arts — first games anniversary history

summary: Psygnosis became strongly associated with visually ambitious Amiga games, elaborate packaging and a distinctive science-fiction and fantasy identity.
note: The CCG archive currently represents only the games already covered on the site, not Psygnosis's complete commercial catalogue.
facts: National Museums Liverpool identifies Psygnosis as a Liverpool studio behind major early PlayStation games and records that Sony closed the studio in 2012.
The Centre for Computing History preserves an extensive Psygnosis catalogue including Commodore Amiga releases such as Shadow of the Beast II, Amnios and Obitus.

sources.label: National Museums Liverpool — Psygnosis studio history
Centre for Computing History — Psygnosis catalogue

summary: Elite Systems Limited was incorporated in England on 14 August 1984. The company began as a developer and publisher for the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64, and its early licensing work included Airwolf before a wider run of licensed and arcade-derived releases.
facts: Elite Systems Limited was incorporated on 14 August 1984.
It began as a developer and publisher for the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64.
Its 1984 licensing activity included an official game based on the television series Airwolf.
note: The incorporation date comes from Companies House; the early platform and licensing details come from Elite's company profile.

Elite Systems — corporate profile

summary: Gremlin Graphics developed and published a broad range of British computer games, including platformers, sports, racing and character-led action titles across the C64 and Amiga years.
note: The archive keeps later company-name variations separate where they were recorded as distinct publisher credits.
facts: The Gremlin Graphics Archive presents an officially endorsed history of the Sheffield-based developer and publisher.
The Centre for Computing History catalogues 82 preserved game records carrying Gremlin Graphics publishing credits across multiple formats.

summary: Sid Meier co-founded MicroProse in 1982. The company became closely associated with simulation and strategy games, and the CCG Commodore archive includes several detailed releases that relied on manuals, maps and patient play.
facts: Sid Meier co-founded MicroProse in 1982.
MicroProse became an important foundation for Sid Meier's later strategy-game work.
The CCG archive records the relevant Commodore releases under the publisher name MicroProse Software.
note: The founding statement is sourced from Firaxis' official studio history; catalogue observations are limited to the games already represented by CCG.

summary: Rainbird was Telecomsoft's premium label, associated with ambitious adventures, simulations and large-format releases that often included extensive supporting material.
note: Rainbird and Firebird are linked here for context but remain separate publisher archives.
facts: The Bird Sanctuary identifies Rainbird as one of Telecomsoft's principal publishing labels alongside Firebird and Silverbird.
The CCG publisher index records two Rainbird-published Amiga games spanning 1987 to 1989.

summary: Virgin Games published and distributed a varied computer-game catalogue across the 1980s and 1990s, spanning original titles, conversions and releases from associated studios and labels.
note: Virgin Games and Virgin Mastertronic remain separate because the archive records them as distinct publishing credits.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves 64 game records published under the Virgin Games name across multiple computer and console formats.
The CCG publisher index currently records 21 Virgin Games releases across Commodore 64 and Amiga, spanning 1983 to 1995.

summary: Thalamus built a focused reputation for technically accomplished Commodore 64 games with strong graphics, music and magazine-era presentation.
note: This summary concerns the games represented in the CCG archive and does not attempt to reproduce a complete company history.
facts: The Centre for Computing History preserves six Commodore 64 games published by Thalamus in its museum collection.
The CCG publisher index currently records five Thalamus C64 releases covering 1986 to 1992.

summary: Americana (or Americana Software) was a budget-priced software label created through a partnership between Mastertronic and U.S. Gold in the mid-1980s.
facts: Americana (or Americana Software) was a budget-priced software label created through a partnership between Mastertronic and U.S. Gold in the mid-1980s. It was set up because U.S. Gold lacked experience in the budget games market and used the label to re-release popular full-price Commodore 64 and other microcomputer games.
note: Americana is additive in CCG: the secondary credit records the Americana release or catalogue relationship and does not overwrite the original publisher stored in the protected game database.
